Corn___Common_Rust.description: Common rust of corn is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It is one of the most frequently occurring foliar diseases of corn and can cause significant yield losses if not managed properly, especially in susceptible hybrids during cool, moist conditions.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongated, powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules are initially light green to yellow, turning cinnamon-brown to dark brown
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing reddish-brown spores (urediniospores)
Severely infected leaves turn yellow, then brown and die prematurely
Pustules may appear on husks, stalks, and leaf sheaths in severe cases
causes: Fungal pathogen: Puccinia sorghi
Favored by cool temperatures (16–23°C) and high relative humidity (>95%)
Windborne spores from infected plants spread the disease rapidly
Overhead irrigation can promote spore germination and infection
Dense plant canopy restricts airflow and maintains moisture
cure: Apply foliar fungicides such as azoxystrobin, propiconazole, or mancozeb at early infection stages
Use systemic fungicides like triazoles (tebuconazole) for better curative action
Remove and destroy severely infected plant debris after harvest
Ensure adequate plant spacing for better air circulation
Apply fungicide spray at 7–14 day intervals during disease-favorable conditions
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Avoid late planting when conditions favor rust development
Apply preventive fungicide sprays at tasseling stage
Maintain field sanitation by removing crop residues
Monitor fields regularly for early disease detection
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes lush growth favorable to disease

Corn___Gray_Leaf_Spot.description: Gray leaf spot (GLS) is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is one of the most economically damaging foliar diseases of corn worldwide, particularly in areas with warm temperatures and high humidity. Under severe conditions, it can reduce grain yield by 30–50%.
symptoms: Rectangular to elongated, tan to gray lesions parallel to leaf veins
Lesions are initially small, water-soaked spots that expand to 1–6 cm long
Lesion edges appear distinct with yellow halos in early stages
Older lesions turn gray to tan with a bleached appearance
Severe infection causes extensive blighting of lower leaves progressing upward
Fine gray fungal sporulation visible on lesions under humid conditions
causes: Fungal pathogen: Cercospora zeae-maydis
Favored by warm temperatures (25–30°C) and prolonged leaf wetness
Survives in infected crop residue on the soil surface
Spores spread by wind and splashing rain
No-till or reduced tillage practices increase inoculum levels
Susceptible hybrids grown consecutively in the same field
cure: Apply strobilurin-based fungicides (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin) at first sign of disease
Use triazole fungicides (propiconazole, tebuconazole) for curative treatment
Mix strobilurin + triazole for broader spectrum control
Apply at tasseling to silking stage for best results
Repeat application every 14–21 days under high disease pressure
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids rated for GLS resistance
Rotate crops with non-host crops like soybeans or small grains
Incorporate or deep-plow crop residues to reduce inoculum
Improve field drainage and air circulation
Apply preventive fungicide sprays before disease onset
Avoid dense planting; maintain recommended plant populations

Corn___Healthy.description: The corn plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease, pest damage, or nutrient deficiency. Healthy corn leaves are vibrant green, smooth, and free from lesions, spots, or abnormal discoloration.
symptoms: Leaves are uniformly green and vigorous
No visible spots, lesions, or pustules
Normal leaf shape and texture
No signs of yellowing or browning
cure: No treatment required
Continue regular crop monitoring
Maintain good agronomic practices
prevention: Continue regular scouting for early disease detection
Maintain optimal soil fertility and moisture
Practice crop rotation each season
Use certified disease-free seeds
Apply balanced fertilization as per soil test recommendations

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight (NLB) is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum (formerly Helminthosporium turcicum). It is a major foliar disease of corn that can cause yield losses of 30–70% in susceptible hybrids under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped lesions 2.5–15 cm in length
Lesions are tan to grayish-green with wavy, irregular margins
Dark, dirty-gray sporulation visible on lesion surface under humid conditions
Lesions may coalesce, causing large areas of leaf blight
Disease usually starts on lower leaves and progresses upward
Severely infected plants show premature leaf death and poor grain fill
causes: Fungal pathogen: Exserohilum turcicum
Favored by moderate temperatures (18–27°C) and prolonged wet periods
Survives in infected corn residue
Conidia spread by wind over long distances
High relative humidity promotes spore germination
No-till farming increases disease risk by leaving residue on surface
cure: Apply foliar fungicides containing azoxystrobin, propiconazole, or pyraclostrobin
Triazole + strobilurin combinations provide best control
Target application at silking when ear leaf and above leaves show symptoms
Spray at 14-day intervals under severe disease pressure
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
prevention: Plant hybrids with race-specific or quantitative resistance to NLB
Rotate corn with soybeans or other non-host crops
Plow crop residue to reduce carry-over inoculum
Apply preventive fungicides at tasseling stage
Improve field drainage and air movement
Avoid excessive plant densities

Potato___Early_Blight.description: Early blight of potato is caused by Alternaria solani. It is a common and widespread foliar disease affecting potato crops worldwide. Despite its name, it typically appears on older, lower leaves during mid- to late-season and can reduce yield and tuber quality significantly.
symptoms: Dark brown to black, circular to irregular spots with concentric rings forming a 'target board' pattern
Lesions are surrounded by yellow chlorotic halos
Disease begins on older, lower leaves and progresses upward
Severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely
Infected stems show dark, sunken lesions
Tubers may develop dark, sunken, dry lesions on the skin
causes: Fungal pathogen: Alternaria solani
Favored by warm temperatures (24–29°C) and alternating wet and dry periods
Survives in infected plant debris and soil
Spores spread by wind, rain splash, and irrigation water
Plant stress due to nutrient deficiency, drought, or disease weakens host resistance
Dense canopy and poor air circulation promote disease development
cure: Apply protectant fungicides: mancozeb, chlorothalonil or copper-based products
Use systemic fungicides: azoxystrobin, propiconazole, or difenoconazole
Apply at 7–14 day intervals starting when plants are 6 inches tall
Remove and dispose of infected plant material
Adjust irrigation to reduce leaf wetness duration
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes
Use resistant or tolerant potato varieties
Rotate potatoes with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 years
Apply balanced fertilization, especially adequate potassium and nitrogen
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or furrow irrigation
Destroy volunteer potato plants and solanaceous weeds

Potato___Healthy.description: The potato plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease or stress. Healthy potato leaves are deep green, turgid, and have a uniform appearance without spots or lesions.
symptoms: Uniformly green, turgid leaves
No visible spots, lesions, or blight
Normal leaf shape without curling or distortion
No signs of wilting or yellowing
cure: No treatment required
Continue regular field monitoring
Maintain good agronomic practices
prevention: Use certified seed potatoes each season
Practice 3–4 year crop rotation
Monitor regularly for early disease detection
Maintain soil health with balanced fertilization
Control weeds and insect vectors

Potato___Late_Blight.description: Late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the most devastating disease of potato. Historically responsible for the Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852), it can destroy an entire potato crop within days under favorable conditions. It is classified as an oomycete (water mold), not a true fungus.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale green to brown lesions on leaf margins and tips
Lesions rapidly expand and turn dark brown to black
White cottony sporulation on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Affected stems show brown to black streaks and rot
Tubers develop firm, reddish-brown rot that spreads inward
Entire plants may collapse and die within a week under severe conditions
causes: Oomycete pathogen: Phytophthora infestans
Favored by cool temperatures (10–25°C) and high humidity (>90%)
Sporangia spread rapidly by wind, rain, and irrigation water
Survives in infected tubers used as seed pieces
Can travel hundreds of kilometers by wind
Pesticide resistance developing in some pathogen strains
cure: Apply metalaxyl or mefenoxam-based systemic fungicides immediately upon detection
Use protectant fungicides: mancozeb, chlorothalonil, copper hydroxide
Apply at 5–7 day intervals during high-risk weather
Remove and destroy affected plants to prevent spread
Haulm destruction (killing vines) 2 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber infection
Never store visibly infected tubers
prevention: Plant only certified, disease-free seed potatoes
Use resistant varieties with Rpi resistance genes
Apply preventive fungicide sprays before disease onset
Avoid overhead irrigation; use furrow or drip irrigation
Destroy culled and volunteer potatoes which harbor the pathogen
Scout fields twice weekly during cool, wet periods
Maintain proper plant spacing for air circulation

Rice___Brown_Spot.description: Brown spot of rice is caused by the fungus Cochliobolus miyabeanus (anamorph: Helminthosporium oryzae / Bipolaris oryzae). It is a major disease of rice in tropical and subtropical regions and caused the devastating Bengal Famine of 1943. It is closely associated with soil nutrient deficiencies, especially potassium and silicon.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval spots with a brown center and yellow to brownish border
Lesions often have a gray or whitish center surrounded by a brown ring
Spots on leaves are 0.5–1 cm in diameter; infected glumes turn dark brown
Severe infection causes leaf blight and premature death
Infected seeds appear brown and shriveled
Seedling blight can occur in heavily infected nurseries
causes: Fungal pathogen: Cochliobolus miyabeanus / Bipolaris oryzae
Favored by temperatures of 25–30°C with high relative humidity
Strongly associated with nutrient-deficient soils (low K, Si, Mn)
Drought stress weakens plants and increases susceptibility
Seed-borne infection
Wind and rain splash spread conidia
cure: Apply fungicides: mancozeb, iprobenfos, edifenphos, or tricyclazole
Foliar spray of potassium silicate to strengthen leaf tissue
Apply balanced NPK fertilizers, especially potassium
Use silicon-rich soil amendments
Seed treatment with thiram or captan before sowing
prevention: Use certified, disease-free seeds
Treat seeds with hot water (52°C for 10 minutes) before sowing
Maintain balanced soil nutrition, especially potassium and silicon
Avoid water stress during crop growth
Plant resistant varieties
Avoid transplanting seedlings from heavily infected nurseries
Destroy infected crop residues after harvest

Rice___Healthy.description: The rice plant is healthy with no visible signs of disease. Healthy rice plants have erect, bright-green leaves with no spots, lesions, or discoloration.
symptoms: Uniformly bright green leaves
No visible spots or lesions
Normal leaf shape and posture
No yellowing or wilting
cure: No treatment required
Continue regular monitoring
Maintain optimal crop management
prevention: Use certified seeds and resistant varieties
Practice balanced fertilization
Maintain proper water management
Monitor regularly for early pest and disease detection
Practice crop rotation where feasible

Rice___Leaf_Blast.description: Leaf blast is the foliar phase of rice blast disease caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae. It is one of the most destructive diseases of rice worldwide, capable of destroying entire crops. The pathogen has hundreds of races, making resistance breeding challenging.
symptoms: Diamond-shaped or spindle-shaped lesions with gray-white centers and brown borders
Lesions have a characteristic spindle shape wider in the middle
Early infections show water-soaked green to gray spots
Lesions expand rapidly under favorable conditions
Severely infected leaves turn completely brown and die
White cottony mycelia visible on lesions in humid conditions
causes: Fungal pathogen: Magnaporthe oryzae
Favored by temperatures of 25–28°C and relative humidity >90%
High nitrogen fertilization promotes lush, susceptible growth
Cloudy weather with dew formation increases infection risk
Conidia are wind-dispersed and highly infectious
Silicon-deficient plants are more susceptible
cure: Apply tricyclazole (a melanin biosynthesis inhibitor) at first symptom appearance
Use isoprothiolane or propiconazole as alternatives
Apply at 7-day intervals during disease-favorable periods
Reduce nitrogen application upon disease detection
Silicon-based fertilizer application strengthens leaf tissue
prevention: Plant blast-resistant varieties (Pi resistance genes)
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization; split N application
Apply silicon fertilizers (calcium silicate) at field preparation
Use certified disease-free seeds; treat seeds with fungicide
Drain fields periodically to reduce humidity
Avoid dense planting; maintain recommended plant spacing
Scout nurseries and transplant fields weekly during vegetative stage

Rice___Neck_Blast.description: Neck blast is the most devastating phase of rice blast disease (Magnaporthe oryzae), attacking the neck of the panicle just below the grain-bearing branches. It can cause complete grain sterility and total yield loss if it occurs early at heading stage. It is considered the most economically important form of blast.
symptoms: Brown to black lesions on the neck of the panicle (just below the first node)
Infected neck becomes brittle and breaks easily
Complete panicle may break off or remain upright but with empty grains
White panicles (panicles without grain) are a characteristic sign
Infected nodes turn dark brown to black
Grain sterility up to 100% in severe cases
causes: Fungal pathogen: Magnaporthe oryzae (same as leaf blast)
Infection occurs at heading stage (most vulnerable period)
Cool temperatures (20–25°C) with high humidity at heading
Splashing rain and dew facilitate spore infection
Late planting increases exposure during susceptible heading stage
High nitrogen application at heading increases susceptibility
cure: Apply tricyclazole or isoprothiolane preventively at boot leaf stage
Apply again at 50% heading to protect panicle emergence
Systemic fungicides (propiconazole, tebuconazole) provide better curative activity
Spraying after neck infection is rarely effective—prevention is critical
Reduce nitrogen top-dressing at panicle initiation stage
prevention: Plant heading-stage resistant varieties
Time planting to avoid cool, humid periods at heading
Apply preventive tricyclazole spray at panicle initiation (PI) stage
Apply second spray at heading (50% panicle emergence)
Avoid excess nitrogen—especially at late growth stages
Use silicon fertilizers to strengthen stem and panicle tissues
Monitor fields daily from PI to heading for early detection

Sugarcane_Bacterial Blight.description: Bacterial blight of sugarcane is caused by Xanthomonas albilineans. It is a devastating systemic vascular disease that invades the xylem tissue, blocking water and nutrient transport. In its acute form, it can rapidly kill entire stools and fields. The disease is also called 'leaf scald' in some regions.
symptoms: White or pale yellow pencil-line stripes running along leaf veins
Stripes may extend the entire leaf length and turn necrotic
Acute phase: rapid wilting and death of leaves ('scalding')
White bacterial exudate visible when cut stalks are squeezed
Internal stalk tissue shows white, cream to pink discoloration
Stunted plant growth and pale yellow-green leaf coloration
Dead central shoot ('dead heart') in young plants
causes: Bacterial pathogen: Xanthomonas albilineans
Spread by infected planting material (setts/billets)
Mechanical transmission via cutting tools (machetes, harvesters)
Wind-driven rain spreads bacteria from leaf to leaf
Aphid vectors can transmit the pathogen
Waterlogged soils increase disease severity
cure: Remove and burn infected stools immediately
Sterilize cutting tools with bleach solution (10%) or flame between stools
Apply copper-based bactericides to reduce spread (limited systemic effect)
Use hot water treatment (50°C for 3 hours) for planting material
Severely infected fields should be fallowed and replanted with resistant varieties
prevention: Plant only certified, disease-free seed cane
Use resistant or tolerant sugarcane varieties
Sterilize all cutting equipment before use
Implement strict quarantine for planting material from disease-endemic areas
Rogue and destroy infected plants promptly
Avoid water logging; improve field drainage
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops between sugarcane cycles

Sugarcane_Healthy.description: The sugarcane plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage. Healthy sugarcane has tall, dark-green leaves with a waxy surface, vigorous growth, and no streaking, spotting, or discoloration.
symptoms: Uniformly dark green, waxy leaves
Vigorous, upright growth
No visible streaks, lesions, or discoloration
Normal leaf shape and structure
cure: No treatment required
Continue regular monitoring
Maintain good agronomic management
prevention: Use certified disease-free planting material
Maintain balanced soil fertility
Practice field sanitation and equipment sterilization
Monitor regularly for signs of disease and pests
Rotate with legumes between sugarcane cycles

Sugarcane_Red Rot.description: Red rot is the most destructive disease of sugarcane, caused by the fungus Colletotrichum falcatum (teleomorph: Glomerella tucumanensis). It attacks the stalk, causing internal rotting that can destroy entire fields. It reduces both cane yield and juice quality, causing major economic losses in South Asia.
symptoms: Reddening of internal stalk tissues when split longitudinally
White patches or spots scattered on the red internal tissue (diagnostic sign)
Fermenting, sour smell from rotted stalks
Drying of leaves starting from the top; leaf midrib turns red
Yellowing and withering of leaves, starting from upper leaves
Shredded internal tissue and hollow stalks in advanced stages
Dark red to black discoloration of nodes
causes: Fungal pathogen: Colletotrichum falcatum
Spread through infected planting setts
Spores spread by wind, rain, and insects (aphids, borers create entry wounds)
Waterlogged or poorly drained soils favor disease
Drought stress followed by rain promotes infection
Mechanical damage from pests or equipment creates entry points
cure: Remove and destroy all infected stools immediately
Treat setts with Bavistin (Carbendazim 0.1%) or Thiram before planting
Apply Propiconazole or Tebuconazole as a soil drench around affected stools
Improve field drainage to reduce waterlogging
Avoid ratoon crop from heavily infected fields—replant with clean material
prevention: Use red rot resistant sugarcane varieties
Plant only disease-free, certified seed cane
Treat setts with hot water at 50°C for 2 hours before planting
Treat setts with Carbendazim (Bavistin) 0.1% for 15 minutes
Improve field drainage; avoid waterlogging
Maintain optimum plant population; avoid over-crowding
Control borer insects that create entry wounds for the fungus
Avoid ratoon cropping in fields with red rot history

Wheat___Brown_Rust.description: Brown rust (also called leaf rust) of wheat is caused by Puccinia triticina (syn. P. recondita). It is the most common and widely distributed rust disease of wheat globally. It can cause yield losses of 10–40% depending on crop growth stage at infection and environmental conditions.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval, orange-brown pustules (uredinia) on leaf surfaces
Pustules are random and scattered, mostly on upper leaf surface
Pustules may also appear on leaf sheaths and glumes
Surrounding leaf tissue turns yellow (chlorotic halo) around pustules
Dark black telia (teliospore) pustules appear on leaves during late season
Severely infected leaves dry out and die prematurely
Yield losses due to reduced photosynthesis and early senescence
causes: Fungal pathogen: Puccinia triticina
Favored by mild temperatures (15–22°C) and high humidity
Urediniospores are wind-dispersed over long distances
Alternate host: Thalictrum species (meadow rue)
Susceptible varieties with no race-specific resistance
Late sowing and delayed maturity extend exposure period
cure: Apply triazole fungicides: propiconazole, tebuconazole, or triadimefon
Strobilurin fungicides (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin) are effective
Use triazole + strobilurin premix for broader control
Apply at flag leaf emergence for best yield protection
Repeat spray at 14–21 days if disease pressure continues
prevention: Plant rust-resistant wheat varieties with Lr genes
Use certified, treated seed free from rust spores
Monitor varieties as new pathogen races may overcome resistance
Apply preventive fungicide at flag leaf stage
Ensure early planting to avoid peak rust conditions
Destroy volunteer wheat and alternate hosts around fields
Participate in regional rust surveillance programs

Wheat___Healthy.description: The wheat plant is healthy with no visible signs of disease. Healthy wheat plants have erect, green leaves without any pustules, spots, or discoloration. They show vigorous growth appropriate to their growth stage.
symptoms: Uniformly green, upright leaves
No visible pustules, spots, or streaks
Normal leaf shape and growth
No yellowing or premature senescence
cure: No treatment required
Continue regular field scouting
Maintain good agronomic practices
prevention: Use certified rust-resistant wheat varieties
Practice timely sowing for your region
Apply balanced NPK fertilizers
Scout fields weekly from tillering to grain fill
Participate in regional pest and disease surveillance

Wheat___Yellow_Rust.description: Yellow rust (stripe rust) of wheat is caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. It is among the most destructive of all wheat diseases, capable of causing yield losses of 70–100% in highly susceptible varieties under epidemic conditions. New virulent races (like Warrior race) have overcome many resistance genes.
symptoms: Bright yellow to lemon-yellow, powdery pustules arranged in stripes along leaf veins
Pustules run parallel to leaf veins in characteristic stripe pattern
Yellow spore masses (urediniospores) cover leaf surface in heavy infections
Cool-weather appearance: often occurs before other rusts
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown and shrivel
Pustules may appear on glumes, awns, and leaf sheaths
Severe infections result in total leaf death and shriveled grain
causes: Fungal pathogen: Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici
Favored by cool temperatures (2–15°C optimal) and moisture
Urediniospores are wind-dispersed; can travel thousands of kilometers
Survives in green wheat tissue year-round in cool regions
Rapidly evolving new virulent races that break down resistance
Dense crop stands and high nitrogen promote epidemic spread
cure: Apply triazole fungicides immediately: tebuconazole, propiconazole, or cyproconazole
Propiconazole is highly effective against stripe rust
Strobilurin + triazole premix provides curative and protectant action
Apply at early symptom stage; delay reduces efficacy significantly
Aerial application may be needed in large-scale epidemics
Apply at 14-day intervals during cool, wet conditions
prevention: Plant varieties with multiple Yr resistance genes
Monitor for new rust races; update variety resistance ratings
Apply preventive fungicide at tillering and flag leaf stages
Early sowing in high-risk areas to mature before peak disease period
Avoid dense planting and excessive nitrogen
Scout fields weekly from tillering onwards in cool seasons
Report unusual rust outbreaks to agricultural authorities
Use regional rust forecast services to plan fungicide timing
